steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on generating alt-text for images on Twitter using the text of the tweet as extra context. Explain the accessibility problem, why this is different from ordinary image captioning, our idea and model, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Visual content on social media and the accessibility problem; alt-text
2. Why alt-text for social media differs from general captioning; our dataset
3. Key idea: use the tweet text as context
4. Background: ClipCap
5. Our approach
6. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Accessibility problem
- sharing/discussing visual content increasingly central to social media
- inaccessible for blind or low vision (BLV) users
- alt-text: HTML attribute, literal natural language description of image content, read by screen reader / braille display
- infrequently included but very important for accessibility
- Twitter lets users write own alt-text (Figure 1) -> burden on users, who often skip it (convenience, lack of awareness)
- as many as 98\% of images on Twitter lack alt-text even after feature rollout
- screen reader just says “Image”
- user-written alt-text quality inconsistent; users not informed about best practices

2. Not just captioning
- long line of research on image captioning; alt-text for social media = special case with own challenges
- good alt-text more explicitly descriptive than high level caption; emphasizes details based on context (Figure 1)
- Twitter image distribution differs from captioning datasets: digital artwork, promotional graphics, screenshots with text
- native “gold” examples vary in quality
- we collect and release first-of-its-kind dataset of image/alt-text pairs from Twitter

3. Context
- social media images come with contextual info that can improve generated alt-text
- often need background knowledge; left image in Figure 1 could be mistaken for stack of books or magazines
- tweet text identifies pamphlets as election flyers
- augment captioning systems with textual conditioning

4. ClipCap
- easily modifiable to accept multimodal inputs; prefix method
- image encoder (CLIP) -> vector embedding -> projected to sequence of embeddings with word-embedding dimensionality
- fed to language model decoder (GPT-2), autoregressively completes caption

5. Our approach (Figure 2)
- add embedding of tweet text to image embedding sequence
- hope: non-overlapping signal -> more accurate captions
- less burden on encoder to distinguish similar object types; decoder gets details hard to get from visual features

6. Contributions
- (1) novel benchmark dataset: images + surrounding textual context
- (2) alt-text method with multimodal conditioning using unimodal language model
- (3) quantitative analysis; beats ClipCap and BLIP-2 by more than 2x on BLEU@4; human evaluation agrees

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Sharing and discussing visual content is becoming a more and more important part of the user experience on social media. But for users who are blind or have low vision (BLV), this kind of content is often not accessible. One solution is alt-text, which is an HTML attribute associated with digital images. It is meant to give a literal natural language description of what is in an image, and it can be read out by a screen reader or a braille display. Alt-text is not included very often, but it is very important for accessibility, because it lets users perceive the content of the image and so have a better experience online. Some social media websites, notably Twitter, have recently let users write their own alt-text for the images they upload (Figure 1 shows an example). However, this puts the responsibility of making the site accessible onto the users, and they often just don't do it, either for convenience or because they are not aware of it. We find that as many as 98\% of images uploaded to Twitter do not have alt-text, even after the feature was widely rolled out, and that is not even counting the quality of the ones that do have it. When a screen reader gets to such an image, it just says “Image”, and the user gets no meaningful information about what the image actually shows. Even when images on Twitter have alt-text written by the user, the quality is inconsistent, since not all users know the best practices.

There is a long line of research on the more general task of image captioning, but alt-text generation for social media is a special case of this task and it has its own challenges. Good alt-text is usually more explicitly descriptive than a high level caption and may emphasize specific details in the image depending on context. Figure 1 shows an example. Also, the types of images on Twitter are quite different from the ones in traditional captioning datasets, and may include digital artwork, promotional graphics, or screenshots that contain text. Another challenge is that Twitter users are not well trained in writing alt-text, so the native “gold” examples can be of very different quality. To support more research in this area, we collect and release a first-of-its-kind dataset of image and alt-text pairs scraped from Twitter.

3. Context
- social media images come with extra contextual information -> can improve automatically generated alt-text
- need background knowledge: left image in Figure 1 may look like a stack of books or magazines
- the post text identifies the pamphlets as election flyers
- so: augment captioning systems with textual conditioning

4. ClipCap
- easy to modify for multimodal inputs; prefix method
- CLIP image encoder -> embedding -> projected to sequence of word-embedding-sized embeddings
- GPT-2 decoder completes sequence autoregressively -> caption

5. Our approach (Figure 2)
- add tweet text embedding to image embedding sequence; non-overlapping signal -> more accurate captions
- encoder doesn't need to distinguish very similar objects; decoder gets details hard to see visually

6. Contributions
- (1) new benchmark dataset with images + textual context
- (2) multimodal conditioning with unimodal language model
- (3) more than 2x better than ClipCap and BLIP-2 on BLEU@4; human evaluation agrees

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Sharing and discussing visual content is becoming a more and more important part of the user experience on social media. But for users who are blind or have low vision (BLV), this kind of content is often not accessible. One solution is alt-text, which is an HTML attribute associated with digital images. It is meant to give a literal natural language description of what is in an image, and it can be read out by a screen reader or a braille display. Alt-text is not included very often, but it is very important for accessibility, because it lets users perceive the content of the image and so have a better experience online. Some social media websites, notably Twitter, have recently let users write their own alt-text for the images they upload (Figure 1 shows an example). However, this puts the responsibility of making the site accessible onto the users, and they often just don't do it, either for convenience or because they are not aware of it. We find that as many as 98\% of images uploaded to Twitter do not have alt-text, even after the feature was widely rolled out, and that is not even counting the quality of the ones that do have it. When a screen reader gets to such an image, it just says “Image”, and the user gets no meaningful information about what the image actually shows. Even when images on Twitter have alt-text written by the user, the quality is inconsistent, since not all users know the best practices.

There is a long line of research on the more general task of image captioning, but alt-text generation for social media is a special case of this task and it has its own challenges. Good alt-text is usually more explicitly descriptive than a high level caption and may emphasize specific details in the image depending on context. Figure 1 shows an example. Also, the types of images on Twitter are quite different from the ones in traditional captioning datasets, and may include digital artwork, promotional graphics, or screenshots that contain text. Another challenge is that Twitter users are not well trained in writing alt-text, so the native “gold” examples can be of very different quality. To support more research in this area, we collect and release a first-of-its-kind dataset of image and alt-text pairs scraped from Twitter.

Our main idea is that even though this domain is challenging, social media images come with extra contextual information, and if this is used properly it can significantly improve the quality of automatically generated alt-text. Images posted on social media often need some background knowledge to caption them well. For example, the left image in Figure 1 could easily be mistaken for a stack of books or magazines. But we actually have a source of text that can give context that is not in the visual information of the image itself, namely the text of the post, which identifies the pamphlets more specifically as election flyers. So we see an opportunity to add textual conditioning to existing captioning systems so they can do better on this hard task.

One model that can easily be changed to accept multimodal inputs is ClipCap. ClipCap uses a prefix method: an image encoder, here CLIP, produces a vector embedding of the image, and this is projected to a sequence of embeddings with the same dimensionality as word embeddings. These embeddings (even though they are not the embedding of any specific language sequence) can then be used as inputs to a language model decoder, here GPT-2, which completes the sequence autoregressively to produce the caption.

Our approach (shown in Figure 2) adds an embedding of the tweet text to the text-like image embedding sequence. We hope that these two sources of information give the decoder signal that is meaningfully non-overlapping, so that it produces more accurate captions. This means the image encoder does not have to be able to tell apart very similar object types, and the decoder gets access to details that may be very hard to get from the visual features.

To summarize, our contributions are: (1) We collect a new benchmark dataset for alt-text prediction on social media that includes both images and the surrounding textual context (2) We introduce a new alt-text generation method that allows multimodal conditioning with a unimodal language model (3) We do a quantitative analysis of this approach on our dataset, and it outperforms prior work on captioning (ClipCap) and vision-and-language pretraining (BLIP-2) by more than 2x on BLEU@4. We also do a human evaluation, which supports these findings.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
An increasingly important aspect of the social media user experience is the sharing and discussion of visual content. However, for users who are blind or have low vision (BLV), this type of content is often inaccessible. One solution to this problem is alt-text, an HTML attribute associated with digital images, which is intended to provide a literal natural language description of an image’s content and can be rendered by a screen reader or braille display. Although it is infrequently included, alt-text is incredibly important from an accessibility standpoint, as it allows users to perceive the content of the image and thus have a better online experience. Some social media websites, notably Twitter, have recently given users the option to write their own alt-text for images they upload (an example is shown in Figure 1). This approach, however, offloads the responsibility of making the site accessible onto the users, who frequently, either for convenience or lack of awareness, simply do not do so [1]. We find that as many as 98\% of images uploaded to Twitter even after the widespread feature rollout do not have alt-text, to say nothing of the quality of those that do. When a screen reader encounters such an image, it simply says “Image”, leaving the user with no meaningful information about what the image actually shows. Even when images on Twitter do have user-written alt-text, the quality is inconsistent, as not all users are well informed about best practices.

Note that while there is a long line of existing research on the broader task of image captioning, alt-text generation for social media is a special case of this task with its own challenges. Well written alt-text is generally more explicitly descriptive than a high level caption and may emphasize specific details in the image based on context [2] (see Figure 1 for an example). Furthermore, the distribution of image types on Twitter differs substantially from those found in traditional captioning datasets, and may include digital artwork, promotional graphics, or screenshots containing text. An additional challenge is that Twitter users are not well trained in writing alt-text, so native “gold” examples can vary substantially in quality. To support continued research in this area, we collect and release a first-of-its-kind dataset of image and alt-text pairs scraped from Twitter.

Our central motivating idea is that despite these challenges, social media images come with additional contextual information that, if properly leveraged, can significantly improve the quality of automatically generated alt-text. Images posted to social media often require some background knowledge to caption adequately. For example, the left image in Figure 1 may easily be mistaken for a stack of books or magazines. However, we do have a source of text that may provide context not present in the visual information of the image itself, namely the text of the post, which more specifically identifies the pamphlets as election flyers. We therefore see an opportunity to augment existing captioning systems with textual conditioning so that they achieve better performance on this challenging task.

One model that is easily modified to accept multimodal inputs is ClipCap [3]. ClipCap uses a prefix method, where an image encoder — in this case CLIP [4] — produces a vector embedding of the image, which is then projected to a sequence of embeddings with the same dimensionality as word embeddings. These (despite not being the embedding of any specific language sequence) can then be taken as inputs to a language model decoder — in this case GPT-2 [5] — which autoregressively completes the sequence to produce the caption.

Our approach (shown in Figure 2) supplements the text-like image embedding sequence with an embedding of the tweet text, in the hope that these two information sources provide meaningfully non-overlapping signal to the decoder and thus more accurate captions. This reduces the burden on the image encoder to distinguish very similar object types, and gives the decoder access to details that may be very difficult to glean from the visual features.

In summary, our contributions are as follows: (1) We collect a novel benchmark dataset for alt-text prediction on social media that includes both images and surrounding textual context (2) We introduce a novel alt-text generation method that allows multimodal conditioning with a unimodal language model (3) We perform a quantitative analysis of this approach on our collected dataset, outperforming prior work on captioning (ClipCap, [3]) and vision-and-language pretraining (BLIP-2, [6]) by more than 2x on BLEU@4. We also conduct a human evaluation that substantiates these findings.

References:

Bigham. “it’s almost like they’re trying to hide it”: How user-provided image descriptions have failed to make twitter accessible. The World Wide Web Conference , 2019.
[2] Kreiss et al. (2022a) Elisa Kreiss, Cynthia Bennett, Shayan Hooshmand, Eric Zelikman, Meredith Ringel Morris, and Christopher Potts. Context matters for image descriptions for accessibility: Challenges for referenceless evaluation metrics.
